Roofing Winston-Salem/Forsyth County School Buildings

Winston-Salem/Forsyth County Schools operates one of the larger public school building portfolios in the Triad, and its roof stock spans everything from 1960s-era gymnasium roofs to recently built elementary wings. School roofing work runs on its own set of rules — the calendar dictates the schedule, public procurement dictates the paperwork, and student safety dictates the site logistics.

Summer-Window Scheduling Around the School Calendar

The gap between the last day of the spring semester and the first day of fall classes is when the bulk of WS/FCS roof replacement happens, and that window is shorter than most owners assume once you subtract time for summer school programs, athletic camps, and facilities maintenance already scheduled in the building. We plan roof projects against the district's actual summer calendar, not a generic assumption about when school is out for the summer, and we build in contingency for weather delays so a project doesn't run into the first week of classes.

Where a full building reroof can't fit inside one summer, we phase it by wing or by roof section across multiple summers, coordinated with the district's facilities office so each phase leaves the building fully weathertight before students return in the fall.

Public Procurement and Bid Requirements for School Roofs

WS/FCS roofing projects run through public bid requirements, and the submittal package has to match that process — itemized unit pricing, prevailing wage documentation where applicable, and product data sheets that let the district's facilities engineer verify the specified system meets the bid's technical requirements before a contract is awarded. We build our bid submissions to that standard from the outset rather than treating public school work like a private commercial quote with extra paperwork bolted on.

  • Roof phasing planned against the district's actual summer calendar, not a generic break
  • Public bid documentation with itemized unit pricing and product data sheets
  • Fenced and signed work zones separated from any active summer programs
  • Structural review before adding rooftop HVAC to older gymnasium and cafeteria decks
  • Weather contingency built into the schedule ahead of the fall semester start
  • Warranty terms aligned with the district's capital asset planning cycle

Gymnasium and Cafeteria Long-Span Roof Decks

Gymnasiums and cafeterias in older WS/FCS buildings typically sit under long-span steel bar joist roofs with wide column spacing, and that structural type has its own considerations when a district wants to add rooftop HVAC equipment that wasn't part of the original design. We run a structural review before specifying any new curb or unit on these roofs, since the added point load from a modern rooftop package unit can exceed what a 1960s or 1970s bar joist system was designed to carry without reinforcement.

Where these long-span roofs are due for membrane replacement rather than equipment additions, drainage is usually the deciding factor in system selection — many of these buildings were designed with fewer roof drains than current code would specify, and we evaluate whether additional drainage needs to be added as part of the reroof rather than just replacing the membrane over an undersized drainage layout.

Safety Protocols With Students and Staff Present

Even during summer break, school buildings host camps, maintenance staff, and administrative personnel, so every school project gets a fenced and clearly signed work zone separating construction traffic from anyone else on campus. Material staging and dumpster placement get planned around the building's active entrances so summer program traffic never crosses the construction zone, and any work that extends into the school year — rare, but it happens on phased multi-summer projects — follows a stricter protocol with supervised access points and coordination with school administration on daily timing.

Warranty Terms School Districts Should Require

Public school districts hold buildings for decades, often the full useful life of the structure, which argues for the longest practical manufacturer warranty term rather than a shorter one chosen to minimize upfront cost. We recommend 20-year No Dollar Limit warranties on TPO systems for most WS/FCS reroofing work, and we document the wind uplift design and fastening pattern against the current code so the warranty holds up if it's ever needed. Closeout documentation, including as-built roof plans and product data sheets, gets delivered in the format the district's facilities asset management system requires.

Questions From District Facilities Staff

Can a full building reroof be completed in one summer?

It depends on the building's size and roof complexity. Smaller elementary buildings often fit in one summer window; larger high schools or buildings needing structural work sometimes need phasing across two summer breaks.

How do you handle bid documentation for public school contracts?

We build submittals with itemized unit pricing, product data sheets, and any prevailing wage or public bid documentation the district's procurement process requires.

Does adding rooftop HVAC to an older gym require structural work?

Often, yes. Bar joist roofs common in older gymnasium and cafeteria buildings weren't always designed for modern package unit loads, so we run a structural review before any new curb goes in.

What happens if weather delays push into the fall semester?

We build weather contingency into the original schedule specifically to avoid this, and if a delay still threatens the start of school, we prioritize sealing the building weathertight over completing cosmetic finish work on schedule.

What warranty term do you recommend for a school roof?

We typically recommend a 20-year No Dollar Limit warranty given how long districts hold their buildings, though the right term depends on the district's specific capital planning horizon for that building.
